rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about task difficulty, the value of each modality, or the benefit of added complexity (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, fusion). The most critical unknown is the performance ceiling of a simple, well-understood single-modality model. 2) What this tests: config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the cleanest, most standard baseline in cellular profiling—RNA features reduced by PCA to 2000 dimensions with no image, no multiprofile, no aggregation, no fusion. It establishes the reference accuracy/F1 that every multimodal or multiprofile configuration must beat to justify its added complexity and computational cost. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: With a limited budget, the highest-information first move is a minimal, fast, interpretable baseline. It (a) calibrates the difficulty of the classification task, (b) provides the anchor for isolating the marginal contribution of the image modality, multiprofile aggregation, and fusion strategy in all subsequent comparisons, and (c) is computationally cheap, leaving budget for follow-up experiments. Without this reference, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_002: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), which establishes a weak baseline. The most foundational uncertainty is whether the RNA representation quality (PCA vs. a learned encoder) is a limiting factor, since every downstream multimodal or multiprofile configuration builds on top of the RNA encoder choice. Question: config_008 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002—only the RNA encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of a learned, low-dimensional (200-d) RNA representation versus a high-dimensional (2000-d) linear one. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is the cheapest way to determine whether learned encoders are worth prioritizing in the remaining budget—if scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA, I can confidently invest in scvi-based multimodal configs; if they are comparable, the bottleneck lies elsewhere (modality, profile, aggregation) and I should pivot to testing image modality next. (2) It changes exactly one variable relative to the baseline, making the comparison interpretable. (3) scvi_n200 appears in the majority of remaining multimodal configurations, so its standalone performance directly informs which multimodal configs are most promising to test next.

Evidence: We have only two completed experiments, both RNA-only single-profile. scvi_n200 (config_008, acc=0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (config_002, acc=0.485), establishing scvi_n200 as the stronger RNA encoder. However, we have zero information on whether the image modality contributes any predictive value. Question: config_004 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) directly tests whether adding a standard image encoder with simple concatenation fusion improves over the best RNA-only baseline (config_008), while keeping the RNA encoder and profile setting identical to isolate the image contribution. Why best: This is the single most critical design decision for a multimodal study—if image adds no value, the entire search space collapses to RNA-only variants. Using the simplest fusion (concat) and a standard encoder (resnet50) avoids confounding the image-contribution question with fusion complexity or encoder capacity. A positive result justifies further exploration of fusion/aggregation; a null result redirects budget to RNA-only multiprofile or encoder comparisons.

Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5362 acc, showing that adding image information to the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200, confirmed by config_008 > config_002) provides a modest ~1.6% gain over RNA-only. However, we have only tested one image encoder (resnet50). Uncertainty: whether a stronger pretrained image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) yields meaningfully better image representations than resnet50, which would affect all downstream multimodal configurations. This experiment (config_009) isolates the image encoder effect by keeping RNA encoder (scvi_n200), profile setting (singleprofile), and fusion (concat) identical to config_004, changing only resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it resolves a fundamental representation question that will inform whether to invest in ViT-based or CNN-based image encoders across many future multiprofile/aggregation experiments, and it is a clean single-variable comparison against an already-completed configuration.

Evidence: scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 for RNA encoding (0.5203 vs 0.4849), and adding an image modality (resnet50 or ViT-L) improves over RNA-only by ~1.5-2%. However, all multimodal results so far use concat fusion; we have no evidence on whether weighted fusion is better or worse. Question: config_026 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + weighted) is a single-variable change from our best config (config_004: concat, 0.5362), isolating the fusion strategy while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: fusion is a fundamental design axis with zero coverage in the history, and resolving it early (weighted vs concat) will inform whether to invest remaining budget in multiprofile/aggregation variants. A single-variable comparison from the current best is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty without confounding multiple factors.

All five completed experiments used singleprofile. The current best (config_026: scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted → 0.540 acc) establishes a strong singleprofile baseline, and we have clear evidence that scvi_n200 > pca_n2000, image adds value over rna_only, and weighted fusion slightly edges concat. The largest unexplored design axis is multiprofile + aggregation. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) keeps RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion identical to the current best, changing only the profile setting and adding the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of multiprofile with minimal added complexity. If avgpool improves performance, it confirms multiprofile adds signal and motivates testing transformer aggregation next; if it does not, it provides evidence that the additional profile dimension is not the bottleneck, redirecting effort toward other axes (e.g., alternative image encoders or RNA encoders like scgpt). Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information experiment because it tests the single biggest untested architectural decision while keeping the comparison as clean as possible.

The dominant finding is the large jump from singleprofile (best: 0.540, config_026) to multiprofile with avgpool (0.678, config_030), indicating that the profile/aggregation axis is the most impactful design dimension. The key uncertainty now is whether avgpool is sufficient or whether a transformer aggregation that models inter-profile interactions yields further gains. Config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_030, changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion, and profile setting constant. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it signals that inter-profile modeling is a productive direction to exploit; if it is comparable or worse, it confirms that simple pooling captures most of the multiprofile benefit and we can redirect effort to other axes (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, isolating the aggregation mechanism in the already-promising multiprofile setting is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: The multiprofile+transformer+weighted multimodal setup (config_020, acc=0.713) is the clear best so far, with a large jump over singleprofile (~0.54). In the singleprofile regime, image encoder choice barely mattered (resnet50: 0.536 vs ViT: 0.532 with concat), but that was a low-performance setting where the image signal was a small additive contribution. In the multiprofile+transformer regime, the image features are being combined with aggregated multi-profile information, and the interaction dynamics may differ substantially. Question: Does swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l (config_010) improve or degrade performance in the high-performing multiprofile+transformer+weighted setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_020, isolating the image encoder effect. Why best next: It tests a fundamental representation choice in the regime where gains are largest, and the answer directly determines whether to invest further in ViT-based pipelines or focus on other levers (aggregation, fusion, RNA encoder). A single-variable change from the current best makes the result interpretable and maximally informative under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_010: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. All completed multiprofile experiments use scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder; scgpt has never been tested in any completed experiment. In singleprofile, scvi_n200 outperformed pca_n2000, but scgpt remains uncharacterized. Question: config_038 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) identical to the current best. This isolates the effect of RNA representation in the top-performing regime. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the incumbent leader, directly testing whether an alternative learned RNA encoder (scgpt) can improve upon scvi_n200 in the setting that already shows the strongest performance. If scgpt matches or exceeds config_010, it opens a new exploitation direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and redirects budget toward other levers (e.g., aggregation or fusion refinements). No other available configuration provides as direct a test of the single largest unexplored variable in the current best configuration.

Evidence: The multiprofile + transformer + weighted pipeline shows a massive jump (~0.71-0.72) over singleprofile (~0.54), and within this regime scvi_n200 (config_010: 0.725) vastly outperforms scgpt (config_038: 0.520), a ~20-point gap. However, pca_n2000 has never been tested in the multiprofile regime. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multiprofile + transformer aggregation pipeline is robust to the RNA encoder choice or whether scvi_n200's learned latent representation is specifically required. Config_017 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is a clean A/B comparison against config_010, changing only the RNA encoder. This is the best next experiment because the RNA encoder question has the largest unresolved uncertainty (scgpt's dramatic failure suggests encoder quality matters, but pca_n2000's position is unknown), the result would clarify whether we can simplify the RNA pipeline, and it directly informs whether further effort should focus on RNA encoder selection or other design dimensions under the limited budget.
